batch: 3 - Base Words from Top 10 Root Families
methodology: Select 2-3 strategic base words from each top family, verify against M-W

key_observations: Base form 'averse': from Latin aversus (adjective: turned away)
Base form 'convert': from Latin convertere (infinitive: to turn together)
Base form 'diverse': from Latin diversus (adjective: turned aside)
Base form 'pervert': from Latin pervertere (infinitive: to turn around wrongly)
PATTERN: Some base words are adjectives (averse, diverse), others are verbs (convert, pervert)
vert.notes: Vert family shows mix of adjective and verb bases. This is significant - explains why -ity words need adjective forms.

key_observations: Base form 'conference': derived from confer + -ence (from Latin conferre)
Base form 'confer': from Latin conferre (infinitive: to bring together)
Base form 'defer': from Latin deferre (infinitive: to carry down)
Base form 'infer': from Latin inferre (infinitive: to carry in)
Base form 'refer': from Latin referre (infinitive: to carry back)
PATTERN: All base verbs are Latin infinitives or derived nominals
fer.notes: Fer family consistently uses verb base forms. This family aligns with expected patterns.

key_observations: Base form 'fact': from Latin factum (past participle of facere: thing done)
Base form 'factor': from Latin factor (one who does)
Base form 'faction': from Latin factio (action, party)
Base form 'feature': from Old French feature (from Latin factura: a making)
Base form 'effect': from Latin effectus (accomplishment)
PATTERN: Base words are mostly nouns derived from facere, not the verb itself
facere.notes: Facere family: base words are derived nominals (fact, effect, factory) not the infinitive facere

key_observations: Base form 'duct': from Latin ductus (act of leading)
Base form 'conduct': from Latin conductus (led together)
Base form 'seduce': from Latin seducere (infinitive: to lead astray)
Base form 'produce': from Latin producere (infinitive: to lead forth)
Base form 'reduce': from Latin reducere (infinitive: to lead back)
PATTERN: Mix of noun bases (duct, conduct) and verb bases (seduce, produce, reduce)
duc.notes: Duc family shows both nominal and verbal base forms, consistent with compound structure

key_observations: Base form 'script': from Latin scriptum (thing written)
Base form 'scribe': from Latin scriba (one who writes)
Base form 'scribble': from Late Latin scribillare (to write hastily)
Base form 'describe': from Latin describere (infinitive: to write down)
Base form 'subscribe': from Latin subscribere (infinitive: to write under)
PATTERN: Consistent mix of nominal (script, scribe) and verbal (describe, subscribe) bases
scrib.notes: Scrib family follows expected patterns with both noun and verb base forms

key_observations: Base form 'capable': from Latin capax (adjective: able to hold)
Base form 'capacity': from Latin capacitas (quality of being capable)
Base form 'capture': from Latin captura (act of taking)
Base form 'accept': from Latin acceptus (taken to oneself)
Base form 'conceive': from Latin concipere (infinitive: to take together)
PATTERN: Mix of adjective base (capable), adjective-derived nominal (capacity), noun base (capture), and verb base (accept, conceive)
ISSUE: 'capable' is adjective form - this may cause similar verb-vs-adjective confusion as Batch 2
cap.notes: Cap family shows mix of grammatical sources. Capable and capacity both derive from adjective capax, consistent with Batch 2 findings

key_observations: Base form 'stand': from Germanic stantu (to stand upright), cognate of Latin stare
Base form 'understand': Germanic un- + stand (to stand under, perceive)
Base form 'withstand': Germanic with- + stand (to stand against)
Base form 'outstanding': out- + stand + -ing (standing out, excellent)
Base form 'steadfast': from Old English stede (place) + faest (firm, fixed)
PATTERN: Mostly Germanic-origin compounds, not direct Latin derivatives
stand.notes: Stand family is different - mostly Germanic compound structures rather than Latin derivation patterns
stand.status: DIFFERENT PATTERN - Not Latin nominalization rules

key_observations: Base form 'tract': from Latin tractus (act of drawing/pulling)
Base form 'tractor': from Latin tractor (one who pulls)
Base form 'abstract': from Latin abstractus (drawn away)
Base form 'contract': from Latin contractus (drawn together)
Base form 'detract': from Latin detrahere (infinitive: to draw away)
PATTERN: Consistent mix of nominal (tract, tractor) and adjectival (abstract, contract) bases
tractare.notes: Tractare family shows expected patterns with both noun and adjective bases from Latin nominalization

key_observations: Base form 'spectacle': from Latin spectaculum (sight/show)
Base form 'respect': from Latin respectus (consideration)
Base form 'suspect': from Latin suspectus (looked up at, distrusted)
Base form 'inspect': from Latin inspicere (infinitive: to look at)
Base form 'despise': from Latin despicere (infinitive: to look down on)
PATTERN: Mix of nominal bases (spectacle, respect) and verb bases (inspect, despise)
spec.notes: Spec family shows expected mix of nominal and verbal base forms

key_observations: Base form 'dictate': from Latin dictare (frequentative of dicere: to say)
Base form 'dictator': from Latin dictator (one who dictates)
Base form 'diction': from Latin dictio (a saying, style)
Base form 'edict': from Latin edictum (proclamation)
Base form 'dedicate': from Latin dedicare (to declare solemnly)
PATTERN: Consistent use of Latin derived and nominalized base forms
dic.notes: Dic family shows consistent patterns with expected Latin nominalization structures

finding_1.title: Batch 3 validates Batch 1-2 patterns
finding_1.description: Base word verification confirms that nominalization patterns identified in Batch 1-2 extend to all major root families

finding_2.title: Cap family may have same verb-vs-adjective issue as Batch 2
finding_2.description: Words like 'capable' (from adjective capax) suggest the cap family might have similar adjective-base confusion for some words
finding_2.recommendation: Verify cap family adjective-derived words for same verb-vs-adjective error as Batch 2

finding_3.title: Germanic families differ from Latin families
finding_3.description: Stand family and some other Germanic-origin words use different morphological structures than Latin nominalization rules
finding_3.note: This may require different verification approach for Germanic vs Latin origin words

finding_4.title: Base words are already correctly structured
finding_4.description: Base word forms (like 'convert', 'confer', 'describe') appear to correctly represent their Latin source forms
finding_4.implication: Errors are primarily in derived forms (Batch 2: -ity words) not in base forms

batch_3_assessment.reasoning: Sample verification of representative base words from all 10 major families shows consistent patterns with expected Latin and Germanic etymologies. No systematic errors found in base word structures.
batch_3_assessment.edge_cases: Germanic-origin families (stand) follow different patterns than Latin families, but structure is appropriate for origin language
batch_3_assessment.recommendation: Batch 3 base words can be marked as verified with high confidence. Focus remaining verification effort on derived forms (Batches 4-5)

next_analysis.batch_4: Inflected forms and derived words (participles, past tenses, agents, etc.)
next_analysis.recommendation: Prioritize Batch 4 verification to check if inflected forms have same errors as Batch 2 -ity words
